---
title: "Physical Compute, Energy, and Infrastructure"
unit_id: "unit-24"
---

## Where the Repository Task Actually Runs

The repository system receives another dependency update. Its cognitive plan
looks simple: retrieve the affected contracts, generate a patch, run tests,
inspect the result, and prepare a rollback.

The plan can run on a laptop in the maintainer's office, across several owned
devices in a personal compute hive, on rented accelerators, or in a centralized
cluster. The logical workflow is similar. The physical consequences are not.

On the laptop, model weights and key-value state exceed accelerator memory.
Layers move between storage, system memory, and the device. Latency rises, but
the repository and credentials remain local. A thermal limit reduces speed
halfway through the test suite.

The hive adds a workstation and a home server. It gains aggregate capacity and
failure alternatives, but now needs identity, scheduling, revocation, network
security, and partition behavior. One device belongs to a family member and may
not receive private project data.

The cloud cluster finishes generation quickly. It pays network latency and
transfer cost, depends on a provider and region, and moves code into a different
trust and jurisdictional boundary. Its efficient accelerator may consume less
energy per token while the facility, cooling, redundancy, and idle capacity
change the total.

"Use 40,000 tokens and two verification passes" is an abstract budget. It says
nothing yet about memory traffic, electricity, water, hardware life, network
dependence, ownership, resilience, or the people who bear the infrastructure's
cost. Cognitive efficiency becomes real only when compiled onto physical
capacity.

## From Cognitive Demand to Physical Demand

Every cognitive action expands into a physical workload. The record should bind
model and artifact identities, precision, context and cache sizes, batch and
sequence shape, generation and verification steps, memory placement, data
movement, storage, network, hardware, site, interval, and required reliability.

Tokens alone are insufficient. Two runs with equal token counts can differ in
model size, active parameters, cache traffic, speculative branches, retrieval,
tool use, and test execution. One may be compute-bound; another spends most of
its time moving data.

The physical compiler begins with demand classes:

- arithmetic and accelerator operations;
- high-bandwidth and ordinary memory capacity;
- storage reads, writes, and endurance;
- network transfer and synchronization;
- CPU orchestration and tool execution;
- power, cooling, and backup requirements;
- space, maintenance, and operator attention.

It then maps them to a hardware profile and records rejected placements. A
route that fits nominal accelerator memory but thrashes through unified memory
is not equivalent to one that remains resident. A route that meets average
power but violates a thermal or battery limit is not feasible.

The map is time-bound. Available memory, temperature, battery, network, other
loads, electricity conditions, and device health change. A profile qualified
at idle can become invalid under concurrent work.

## Memory Movement Can Dominate

Model discussions often focus on arithmetic throughput. Inference and training
also move weights, activations, optimizer state, cache, retrieval results, and
artifacts through a hierarchy of storage, memory, interconnects, and networks.

When the model does not fit, the system can shard by layer or tensor, offload to
CPU or disk, compress weights or cache, reduce context, use sparse activation,
or select a smaller route. Each choice trades latency, throughput, fidelity,
energy, endurance, and implementation complexity.

The repository task is interactive. A method optimized for large batches may
show high throughput while delivering an unusable first-token delay. Disk
offload may make a model fit yet extend the review beyond the human's available
window. A smaller model plus retrieval and verification may complete sooner and
with stronger evidence.

Data movement belongs in the resource receipt. It should report bytes by tier,
transfer paths, cache reuse, compression, recomputation, and stalls. Otherwise a
claimed compute reduction can hide increased memory traffic or network burden.

Storage is not free archival space. Repeated model paging and checkpoint writes
consume bandwidth and device life. Recovery copies improve resilience while
increasing capacity and embodied replacement pressure. The correct comparison
is end to end.

## Hardware Profiles Are Versioned Decisions

A runtime should not infer a permanent machine class from a device name. Two
systems with the same nominal accelerator can differ in memory, thermal design,
storage, driver, background load, power mode, and failure history.

A hardware profile records observed capacity and the policy used to interpret
it. It can include accelerator and CPU identity, usable memory by tier, transfer
bandwidth, storage behavior, supported kernels and precision, thermal envelope,
battery, network, meter coverage, and known defects. The record names the probe,
time, environment, uncertainty, and expiry.

Candidate execution profiles are tested in stages. A dry allocation checks fit.
A bounded kernel test checks compatibility. A short workload observes memory,
temperature, and throughput. A canary checks end-to-end output and recovery.
Rejected profiles remain visible so the system does not repeat a dangerous
experiment every time it restarts.

Dynamic adaptation needs hysteresis. If the runtime switches placement whenever
temperature crosses one noisy reading, it can oscillate between profiles and
lose more work than it saves. Entry and exit thresholds, minimum dwell time,
cooldown, and state-safe handoff belong to the decision.

Pressure should reduce optional work before required safety work. The system can
shrink batch size, reduce speculative branches, move a cache, or fall back to a
smaller model. It should not silently disable verification or monitoring because
those components consume memory.

Hardware probes do not grant authority. Discovering a fast device does not
permit the system to send it private data, install software, spend money, or run
in the background. The profile supplies capability evidence to a later policy
decision.

Profiles also make regressions diagnosable. A slower result can be attributed to
a changed driver, thermal limit, storage mode, or workload rather than vaguely
to the model. Material changes invalidate the receipt and trigger bounded
requalification.

## Measure Use Before Modeling Impact

Physical accounting separates observed use from modeled consequence.

Observed quantities can include wall time, device utilization, memory traffic,
network bytes, node power, facility energy, temperature, cooling operation, and
failures. Each needs a meter identity, scope, interval, sampling policy,
calibration, missing-data rule, and uncertainty.

Modeled quantities translate observations into attribution, emissions, water,
cost, or lifecycle impact. They add assumptions about facility overhead,
electricity mix, marginal versus average generation, cooling, shared capacity,
hardware allocation, and supply chain.

The two should never be collapsed. A meter reading of server power does not
directly measure the workload's global emissions. A regional average does not
reveal the marginal source at that hour. A facility power-usage factor does not
describe every cooling condition.

The receipt can state:

> During interval I, meter M observed energy E for node set N. Facility and
> lifecycle impacts were estimated with model V under assumptions A, exclusions
> X, and uncertainty U.

This sentence is less dramatic than "the model used E clean energy," but it can
be audited and revised.

Missing backup or cooling energy should remain missing, not silently become
zero. Shared infrastructure requires an explicit allocation rule. The same
measured facility total can support different workload attributions, so the
model version belongs beside the result.

## Useful Output Is the Denominator

Lower energy per token is not enough if the route needs more tokens, retries,
verification, or repair. Lower energy per run is not enough if the run produces
fewer accepted useful outcomes.

The relevant ratio is claim-specific: physical resources per accepted patch,
per verified decision, or per recovered incident under a fixed quality and
authority contract. Unsafe or unusable outputs do not count as useful delivery.

The local laptop may consume more joules per generated token but avoid transfer,
provider, and review overhead. The cluster may finish more quickly and reduce
energy per accepted patch. The hive may reuse otherwise idle owned hardware yet
spend more coordination and standby energy.

All attempts remain in the denominator. A central route that retries failed
workers, a local route that recompiles after thermal interruption, and a hive
route that requeues after device dropout all pay those costs.

Efficiency can increase total impact through greater demand. A cheaper task can
be run more often, at larger scale, or on work that was previously rejected.
The system should report unit efficiency and total consumption separately. It
should not infer that one controls the other.

## Energy Is Capacity, Timing, and Reliability

Electricity is not only a scalar cost. The workload needs capacity at a place
and time, with quality and continuity sufficient for its purpose.

Training can sometimes shift across hours or locations. Interactive inference,
incident response, and human review have tighter deadlines. A flexible workload
can pause or reduce precision when the grid is constrained; a safety monitor may
not be allowed to disappear.

The run contract names deadline, interruptibility, checkpoint interval,
recovery, minimum service, and degradation. A scheduler can prefer lower-impact
windows only after policy and usefulness constraints are satisfied.

Backup power and redundancy improve availability while adding equipment, idle
loss, maintenance, and fuel. A facility's normal-operation efficiency does not
establish resilience during grid, cooling, or network failure.

Power loss tests should follow effects. If the repository generator stops, can
the task restart from complete state? Did a partial migration occur? Are
credentials still bounded? Is a human available to interpret the residual? A
checkpoint file alone does not prove recovery.

## Water, Land, Materials, and Hardware Life

Operational electricity is one infrastructure axis. Cooling water, land,
construction, accelerators, memory, networking, batteries, critical materials,
transport, maintenance, reuse, and retirement also matter.

Accounting should avoid both omission and false precision. Facility water use
depends on cooling design, climate, season, and electricity generation. Hardware
impact depends on manufacturing, utilization, lifetime, replacement, and
allocation among workloads. Supply-chain visibility is incomplete.

The chapter does not require every task to carry a perfect lifecycle inventory.
It requires consequential decisions to preserve known categories, uncertainty,
and excluded burdens. A hardware refresh justified by energy efficiency should
include embodied replacement and e-waste. Extending old device life should
include its lower performance, reliability, and security support.

Local context matters. One unit of water or power has different consequences in
different regions and seasons. A global average can hide a stressed community.
Community impact includes prices, infrastructure competition, noise, land use,
employment, tax arrangements, and who participates in the decision.

These are not properties that a scheduler can optimize from telemetry alone.
They require institutional authority, affected-party evidence, and contestable
judgment.

## Concentration Changes the Architecture

Frontier accelerators, high-bandwidth memory, fabrication, advanced packaging,
cloud platforms, power interconnection, and skilled operations are concentrated
resources. Concentration can improve utilization and reliability while creating
dependency, bargaining power, surveillance, and correlated failure.

A centralized provider may offer excellent hardware, mature networking, rapid
recovery, and lower unit cost. The stack should use those advantages when they
fit the authority and resilience contract. It should not confuse operational
quality with user ownership or exit.

The infrastructure record names provider, region, jurisdiction, portability,
data exposure, model and artifact custody, price risk, quota, failure domain,
and exit path. A nominally portable workload may depend on proprietary services,
accelerator behavior, or data gravity that makes exit slow.

## Infrastructure Is a Governance Surface

Compute access determines who can train, evaluate, deploy, and reproduce a
system. Allocation policies therefore shape the research and institutional
landscape even when the scheduler appears purely technical.

Quota, pricing, identity requirements, acceptable-use rules, export controls,
interconnection queues, and provider moderation can block or privilege work.
Some controls may reduce harm; others may concentrate power or exclude legitimate
users. The stack should record the authority and appeal path rather than
presenting denial as a law of physics.

Hardware attestation and metering can support compute-policy enforcement. Their
coverage is bounded. A trusted report about one device state does not prove the
software, workload, operator, or downstream effects. Attestation roots create
update, revocation, compatibility, surveillance, and capture risks of their own.

Infrastructure governance should preserve least disclosure. A provider may need
evidence that a job fits a resource or policy envelope without receiving the
job's private content. Selective proofs, secure measurement, and local
enforcement can reduce exposure, but each adds a trust and failure surface.

Exit is a resilience control. Models, checkpoints, manifests, logs, and recovery
procedures should remain portable enough for the declared fallback. A paper
right to leave is weak if moving petabytes, rebuilding kernels, or requalifying
every evaluator takes months.

Public policy claims require separate evidence. The architecture can expose
concentration, dependencies, denials, and switching cost. It cannot decide the
correct market structure or legal remedy by itself.

Competition analysis is evidence about markets and institutions, not a proof
that centralization is always harmful. The engineering question is whether the
system retains meaningful alternatives and can test recovery from provider
loss.

## Personal Compute Hives

A personal compute hive joins devices owned or authorized by a person,
household, workshop, or project into a governed resource field. It may include a
laptop, workstation, phone, home server, storage node, or explicitly leased
external worker.

Reachability is not permission. Every node has an owner or guardian, hardware
profile, attestation state, allowed data and tool classes, energy and thermal
constraints, availability, trust tier, and revocation path.

Every job has a principal, purpose, data class, tools, effect envelope,
deadline, risk and spending limits, acceptance test, and cleanup obligation.
The scheduler intersects job and node policy before optimizing latency, cost,
energy, or locality.

This order matters. A fast rented node is ineligible for private family data
unless an explicit contract permits that exposure. A child's device may be
reachable but blocked from adult project work. A phone can approve a high-risk
job without becoming the execution authority.

Among eligible nodes, the hive chooses the least-authority adequate placement.
It binds a task-local context and execution lease, monitors the run, and emits
artifact, effect, resource, recovery, and residual receipts.

The goal is not to use every idle cycle. It is to make owned capacity available
without turning a household network into an unbounded cluster.

## Locality Is More Than Latency

Keeping computation near the data can reduce network transfer, improve response
time, preserve operation during provider outages, and limit exposure. It can
also place sensitive work on poorly maintained devices with weak isolation and
irregular backups.

Locality should be stated by object and stage. Source files may remain local
while a redacted embedding or public dependency graph travels. Generation may
run remotely while final evaluation and effect authority remain on the owned
machine. A result can return without granting the worker access to the repository.

Data minimization happens before routing. The system selects the smallest input
that can support the task, marks derivation and reidentification risk, and binds
retention and deletion. Redaction is not automatically safe; code structure,
paths, errors, and embeddings can reveal private information.

Confidential-computing mechanisms may reduce provider visibility, but they do
not eliminate side channels, compromised roots, malicious clients, output
leakage, or governance questions. Their evidence should narrow the exposure
claim rather than turn an external node into a local one.

Local operation can also preserve user agency. A person can inspect resource
use, revoke a lease, keep a model available after a service changes, and choose
when a device works. Those benefits depend on usable controls, software support,
and real ownership. A technically local system controlled by a remote account
or opaque update path may offer little practical exit.

The placement decision therefore balances latency, transfer, privacy, security,
maintenance, continuity, and authority. "Local first" is a default to test, not
a universal answer.

## Federation Adds a Principal Boundary

Two hives or a personal hive and a project cluster can cooperate through a
federation lease. The lease names principals, job, data and tool scope, sandbox,
resource budget, evidence, expiry, revocation, cleanup, and dispute path.

The external node should not discover private network resources merely because
it accepted one job. Results return through a narrow artifact interface. Local
secrets and credentials remain outside the lease unless explicitly required and
authorized.

Reputation can inform scrutiny but cannot grant authority. A well-behaved node
still needs a current lease. A new node can execute a low-risk public job if it
satisfies the contract without inheriting broad distrust forever.

Payment and bidding come after policy. An ineligible node cannot win by being
cheap. Estimates should include expected latency, energy, network, failure,
verification, and recovery rather than compute price alone.

Federation creates legal, tax, labor, consumer-protection, and jurisdictional
questions beyond the scheduler. The technical lease can expose the relationship;
it cannot decide the applicable institution.

## Partitions Are Authority Events

Distributed systems must choose how to behave when communication is delayed or
lost. For ordinary cached data, availability may be preferred. For revocation
and authority, acting on stale state can create irreversible effects.

Suppose the workstation loses contact with the hive authority after receiving a
job. A previous grant appears valid locally, but the principal may have revoked
it. The safe action depends on the job's effect envelope and prospective policy.
Read-only public analysis may continue under a lease; a private-data mutation
may quarantine before action.

The system should record last confirmed authority, partition time, allowed
offline actions, no-mutation evidence, residual owner, and reconciliation path.
On reconnection it compares effects with current authority. It does not rewrite
history to imply continuous authorization.

This can reduce availability. That is an explicit trade, not a scheduler bug.
The policy should reserve offline capability for cases whose consequences are
acceptable under stale authority and test that boundary.

## Resilience Requires Diverse Failure Domains

More nodes do not automatically create resilience. Devices may share power,
network, software, credentials, model artifacts, or operator mistakes. Three
machines in one room are not three independent sites.

The repository workflow maps dependencies: model storage, source repository,
package mirrors, credential service, evaluator, approval channel, and backup.
A recovery plan should survive the failure classes it names.

Hive dropout can requeue a pure generation job. A stateful test or migration
needs checkpoint and effect reconciliation before another node continues.
Duplicate execution can be worse than delay.

Central infrastructure can provide stronger redundancy than a home hive. A
local route can continue during provider outage. A hybrid design may keep
private context and authority local while using external capacity for public,
sandboxed computation.

Resilience comparisons include recovery time, lost work, state correctness,
operator burden, security updates, replacement parts, and residual effects. A
route that remains online but acts from stale authority is not resilient in the
relevant sense.

## Maintenance Is Part of Capacity

Hardware does not remain available by owning it. Devices need updates, keys,
monitoring, cleaning, replacement, compatible drivers, tested backups, and
someone who can diagnose failure. A hive that relies on unpaid household labor
has not made that cost disappear.

The capacity record should include maintenance windows, support horizon, spare
parts, recovery competence, and the operator's sustainable workload. Unsupported
software can turn useful old hardware into a security liability. Frequent
replacement can improve reliability while increasing cost and embodied burden.

Automation can reduce routine work, but it also needs authority limits. An
updater should not rewrite every node during a partition, invalidate the only
recovery image, or expand remote access to simplify administration. Staged
rollout, diversity, rollback, and an offline recovery path preserve options.

Human capacity is a failure domain. If one person holds every key and procedure,
the system is not resilient to their absence. Documentation, rehearsed recovery,
and scoped delegation are physical-infrastructure controls because they
determine whether hardware can return to useful service.

Maintenance debt should therefore travel with every placement decision, not
appear later as an unexplained loss of capacity.

## Beyond Digital Accelerators

Neuromorphic, photonic, analog, in-memory, and quantum approaches may change
physical tradeoffs. They should enter through the same end-to-end contract.

A device-level operation count or energy result does not establish application
advantage. The comparison includes data encoding, conversion, memory, control,
error correction, training, host computation, networking, programmability,
yield, reliability, verification, and fallback.

Workload fit matters. Event-driven hardware may excel on sparse temporal
signals without replacing dense language-model inference. Photonics may offer
high-throughput linear operations while conversion and control dominate another
stage. Quantum advantage claims need classical baselines, data-loading cost,
noise, scale, and complete output quality.

Alternative substrates should not inherit authority from novelty. They need
hardware identity, measurement, error envelope, update and revocation policy,
security analysis, and a route back to a qualified baseline.

## One Workflow, Three Placements

The team freezes the repository task and compares local, hive, and centralized
routes under the same acceptance test and authority ceiling.

The local route uses a compact model, retrieval, and full tests. It keeps data
and credentials on the workstation. Memory offload raises latency and the run
throttles once, but it completes without network dependence.

The hive route sends public dependency analysis to the home server and keeps
private source generation on the workstation. The phone supplies a bound review
approval. A simulated partition revokes the server lease; the public analysis
finishes under its offline policy while the private action quarantines. The
team counts requeue and reconciliation.

The cluster route sends a redacted task to a rented accelerator. It is fastest
for generation, but repository retrieval, result verification, and effect
authority remain local. The provider route loses eligibility when the patch
requires an unredacted secret-bearing file.

The comparison reports accepted outcome, wall time, compute, memory and network
traffic, measured energy where available, modeled impact with uncertainty,
money, human work, failures, recovery, privacy exposure, and residuals. No route
wins by one number.

The decision may differ by task. That is the point of infrastructure-aware
routing.

## Failure Modes

**Token physicalism.** Token count is treated as complete resource use.

**Arithmetic tunnel vision.** Accelerator operations hide memory and network
movement.

**Fit as performance.** Making a model load is reported as useful throughput.

**Meter-to-impact leap.** Node energy becomes a global environmental claim.

**Missing as zero.** Cooling, backup, or supply-chain burdens disappear.

**Unit-efficiency morality.** Better energy per token is treated as lower total
impact.

**Embodied amnesia.** A hardware refresh ignores manufacturing and retirement.

**Global-average locality.** Regional and community constraints vanish.

**Reachability as authority.** Every discovered device becomes an eligible
worker.

**Optimization before policy.** Price or speed chooses a forbidden node.

**Reputation as permission.** Historical behavior replaces a current lease.

**Partition optimism.** Stale grants continue irreversible work.

**Replica resilience.** Correlated devices are counted as independent recovery.

**Novel-substrate exceptionalism.** Component results bypass end-to-end
accounting.

## The Strongest Simpler Baseline

The strongest baseline runs the task on one well-administered local machine or
one mature cloud provider. It uses ordinary monitoring, access control,
backups, cost reports, and regional sustainability data. It avoids a custom
hive scheduler and detailed per-task lifecycle accounting.

That baseline may be more reliable and secure. A personal hive increases
attack surface and maintenance. Fine-grained impact estimates can consume more
effort than they improve decisions.

The wider layer earns its cost only when physical constraints materially change
placement, accepted useful output, privacy, resilience, or whole-lifecycle cost.
It should be compared with competent local, cloud, and hybrid baselines under
real failure and workload conditions.

If a static placement and ordinary accounting match the outcomes at lower
burden, use them.

## What the Current Work Establishes

Personal Compute Hives currently has seven public record schemas, two valid and
eight invalid admission fixtures, three valid and six invalid partitioned-
authority records, 52 live family declarations, and a 31-declaration reachable
refinement. Its independent consumer executes six accepted events, checks seven
trace splits, covers 47 finite routes, rejects all post-closure events, and
rejects all 144 authored mutations.

Those artifacts establish finite record, custody, policy-first, lease,
partition, and route consequences. No live scheduler, registry, portal,
authority service, network overlay, sandbox, federation, partition experiment,
energy measurement, dropout recovery, privacy, security, availability, useful
work, independent reproduction, or transfer ran.

Physical Compute Infrastructure implements a 36-declaration Lean surface over
a six-transition review and 44 admission-axis mutations with exact repairs. It
proves finite accounting, capacity, monotonicity, receipt invalidation, and two
information-loss constructions. It does not measure a natural workload or
establish performance, environmental impact, resilience, community outcome,
deployment readiness, or infrastructure superiority.

Both chapter cores remain at argument support. Source-reported infrastructure
and hardware results are comparators, not local reproduction.

## From Minimum Measurement to Governed Infrastructure

A minimum implementation can run the repository workflow on one local node and
one isolated external node. Freeze the task and authority. Measure wall time,
memory, storage and network traffic, node energy, failures, human work, and
accepted outcomes. Preserve assumptions and missing facility data.

Add a policy-first scheduler with one private and one public data class. Inject
thermal pressure, memory exhaustion, network loss, stale authority, revocation,
node dropout, corrupted output, and incomplete cleanup. Verify denial,
quarantine, requeue, effect reconciliation, and residual custody.

The next stage compares local, hive, central, and hybrid routes across natural
workloads with matched models and acceptance tests. It needs independent meters,
evaluators, security review, privacy analysis, lifecycle estimates, and affected-
community evidence where claims extend that far.

A mature system would compile cognitive demand onto live hardware and
infrastructure profiles, filter placements through rights and authority, route
across diverse failure domains, account for complete physical and human cost,
shift flexible work under capacity constraints, recover effect-complete state,
and preserve the uncertainty between measured use and modeled impact.

It would not maximize distributed compute. It would choose the smallest
physical commitment that satisfies the task and its social contract.

## The Strongest Objection

Physical-impact accounting is highly context-dependent. Grid conditions,
facility allocation, supply chains, water, and community effects often lie
outside the system's observation or control. Detailed estimates can create
false precision and distract from direct capability and safety work.

The objection is correct. The layer should expose uncertainty and use decision-
relevant resolution, not pretend to produce a universal footprint. It should
not claim that architecture alone solves institutional allocation or
environmental justice.

The narrower claim is operational: physical capacity and topology can change
whether a cognitive plan fits, who controls it, how it fails, and what it costs.
Those differences deserve explicit evidence when they affect a decision.

## Evidence That Would Change the Conclusion

This layer should narrow if matched deployment studies show that physical
constraints and topology do not materially affect accepted useful output,
latency, privacy, resilience, recovery, or total cost, or if ordinary provider
reports produce equally good decisions with less burden.

Support would require natural multi-site workloads, calibrated meters,
transparent impact models, strong local and cloud baselines, failure injection,
security and privacy evaluation, authority and partition tests, lifecycle and
community boundaries, independent reproduction, and transfer across devices,
networks, regions, providers, and time.

Formal proofs can establish finite accounting and authority invariants. They
cannot establish meter accuracy, grid effects, supply-chain truth, community
benefit, privacy, useful scheduling, or resilience in deployment.

## What This Establishes

Cognitive budgets become physical demand through memory, storage, network,
hardware, power, cooling, reliability, and human operations. Measured use and
modeled impact are different evidence. Useful accepted output, not tokens alone,
is the denominator.

Central clusters, local machines, personal hives, and federated workers offer
different ownership, locality, capacity, and failure properties. Policy and
authority must filter placement before optimization. Partitions, revocation,
dropout, and recovery are part of the architecture.

The repository contains bounded finite controls for hive admission and physical
accounting. It does not establish a deployed hive or an environmentally
superior infrastructure.

Once the stack can distribute work and modify its own mechanisms, physical
capacity also becomes a channel for replication and self-expansion. Unit 25
confronts recursive improvement, replication, and containment directly.
